MGT 409 · AI Foundations for Managers · Fall 2026 · Final project

Lane League

A one-minute supercar drive that gives a stressed student a break with a hard edge. Three AI agents make the minute personal, and the server, not a model, keeps the score.

Renae Wen

1 · Title and links

GitHub repo (public, clone this)https://github.com/doraemon-creator/lane-league
AppRuns locally from a fresh clone in about two minutes. The README is the runbook: Python 3.10+, pip install -r requirements.txt, start with uvicorn, open http://127.0.0.1:8000. The key is read from .env in the repo or one folder up. Not hosted.
What it doesYou pick one of sixteen supercars and drive for sixty seconds; a steward agent and a passenger agent open the minute with a note about your car, the weather, and how you feel, and a clerk agent closes it with your result, your trend, and one tip, while the server recounts every coin from your drive so the leaderboard stays honest.

2. Motivation

Who has the problem. A business-school student in recruiting season. The day is a coffee chat, a case drill, a problem set, and another email from a firm. Between them there are many short gaps, and the break people actually take in those gaps is the phone. A feed or a group chat has no end, so a two-minute pause has no edge, and the next block of work starts late and scattered. Three classmates in exactly this situation are the users behind this project (Section 7).

What it costs today. The cost is not money. It is recovery and focus. Two pieces of research frame it:

  • A 2022 meta-analysis of 22 samples (2,335 people) found that micro-breaks of ten minutes or less raise vigor (d = 0.36) and reduce fatigue (d = 0.35). The effect on task performance was small and not significant overall, so I claim recovery, not productivity. Albulescu et al., “Give me a break!”, PLOS ONE 17(8): e0272460, 2022.
  • In an experiment with 414 people solving word puzzles, those who took their break on a phone were as depleted afterwards as people who took no break at all, and did worse than people whose break was on a computer or on paper. Kang & Kurtzberg, “Reach for your cell phone at your own risk”, Journal of Behavioral Addictions 8(3): 395–403, 2019.

Why care. Short breaks help when they are real breaks, and the default break is the one that helps least. A break that is short, absorbing, and guaranteed to end can be taken five times a day without stealing the afternoon. That is the whole product: a minute with an edge.

3. What is new here

I looked at what a student would reach for instead.

Existing optionWhat it doesWhat Lane League does differently
Calm, HeadspaceGuided audio. You listen and stay still. Built around a library of sessions and a streak.You steer. Your hands and eyes are busy, which is the point when your head is loud. It cannot run past sixty seconds.
Instagram, TikTok, group chatsThe default phone break. Endless by design.A hard stop. The minute ends on the clock, then a results page with one tip, then you are done.
Mario Kart, Gran Turismo, mobile racersBuilt to keep you playing: another cup, another season, another level.One car, one road, one minute. No unlocks and no reason to stay.
Forest and other focus timersReward you for not touching the phone while you work.They guard the work block; Lane League is the break between blocks, so the two fit together.
ChatGPT as a “calm friend”Talks as long as you type. Will invent a score if asked, and can be talked into things.The agents speak about your actual car, weather, and record, but they cannot mint points: the server recounts the drive and posts its own number.

Short browser racing games exist, and so do leaderboards. What I have not found is the combination: a break that is hard-capped at sixty seconds, personal (the crew reads your car, your record, the weather, and a line about how you feel), social (a shared board), and trustworthy (the score is recomputed by the server from the drive itself, so a board among classmates cannot be gamed by a prompt or by editing a request). The user feedback added one more difference I now design for on purpose: the crew does not talk about work, recruiting, or studying. The minute is a break from them.

4. The agents

Lane League has three agents. All three run on gpt-6-luna through Portkey on the course key. Everything that must be exact (the firewall, the road, the score, the caps) is ordinary server code, not a model. That split is the main design choice: models are used for the parts that benefit from language and from reading context, and nothing a model says can change a number.

Figure 1. How one ranked minute flows. Red boxes are model agents; gray boxes are server code with no model; dashed boxes run in the browser.

AgentJobToolsReturns
StewardOpens the minute. The only agent that sees the driver's free-text note.lookup_car (the car's numbers), driver_card (earlier minutes, best score), track_card (road, weather, what the weather does), ask_passenger (handoff)A coach note (≤240 characters) that names the car and the weather and gives one cue, plus the passenger's radio line
PassengerRides along with one calm radio line. Never sees the driver's note; it gets only the one sentence the steward hands over, after the server scans it.passenger_brief (car, road, weather)One line ≤120 characters
ClerkCloses the minute. Reads the server's count and the driver's history, posts the points, reads the board.official_result, driver_history, commit_result (takes no point argument), standingsHeadline, two sentences, one concrete tip for the next minute, and a rank line

Who hands work to whom. The server's firewall runs first and can stop the minute before any model is called. The steward calls its three lookup tools in one turn, then hands one sentence to the passenger through ask_passenger; the server scans that sentence before the passenger sees it. After the drive, the server recounts the minute, and only then does the clerk run. The steward and the clerk never talk to each other: the clerk's inputs are the server's count and the database, so a strange coach note cannot leak into the score.

Why this model and these settings. The course key allows only gpt-6-luna, and the jobs are short: follow a tool order, read small JSON, write two sentences. Reasoning effort is none. That is required, not just cheap: when I tried low, the endpoint refused every tool-using request with “Function tools with reasoning_effort are not supported for gpt-6-luna-global in /v1/chat/completions.” Each agent has a request cap and a tool-call cap (Figure 1), so a confused agent stops instead of looping.

One real ranked minute, step by step

This is one ranked minute from the measured set. Driver “Avery Cole”, Ferrari 296 GTB, with the note “Long day of case prep. I need one minute.” The driving was scripted so I could repeat the run and take screenshots at fixed moments. Every agent call, token count, and score below is real output from the app.

  1. Server firewall. The name and the note passed the injection check, so the server built today's road from a random seed: Harbor Hairpin, wet.
  2. Steward, turn 1, three tools at once. track_card returned “Harbor Hairpin, Wet. It is wet, so the same wheel does less. Lift earlier.” lookup_car returned 179 mph, grip 0.70, steering 1.85. driver_card returned no earlier minutes.
  3. Handoff. The steward called ask_passenger with “Ferrari 296 GTB on a wet road—what would you say?” The server scanned it and passed it on. The passenger called passenger_brief and answered: “Wet pavement glistens through the Harbor Hairpin; the 296's sharp nose calls for a gentle turn.”
  4. Steward, final answer. Coach note: “Long day of case prep—set it down for this minute. In the Ferrari 296 GTB on the wet road, lift earlier and keep the turn gentle; low grip means the sharp nose can slide.” It acknowledges the feeling in a few words and moves to the car. The server checked that every number in it came from a tool. Time from click to road: 11.2 s.
  1. The drive. The browser drives the server's road and records a trail point every 0.1 s, plus one on every frame that passes a coin or a hurdle. At the end it sends the trail, not a score.
  2. Server recount. The server rebuilt Harbor Hairpin from the seed and replayed the trail: 10 of 14 coins, 1 hurdle, crossed the line with 17.99 s left. 10 × 100 − 25 + 250 + 144 = 1,369. The browser's own count matched exactly.
  3. Clerk, turn 1. official_result, driver_history, and commit_result together: read 1,369, found no earlier minutes, posted 1,369. Turn 2. standings: rank 1.
  4. Clerk, final answer. “Avery Cole scores 1,369 points. Avery took 10 coins, hit 1 hurdle, and crossed the finish line. This was Avery's first minute.” Tip: “Try to collect the 3 missed coins on the right next minute.” The clerk's number matched the board's, so nothing was replaced.

5. Tokenomics

Prices. gpt-6-luna list prices from the course tools: input $0.10, cached input $0.01, cache write $0.125, and output $0.50 per million tokens. The app prices every run with that formula, stores it, and shows it on the results page (Figure 5) and in the garage's Crew budget panel.

Per user and at scale. A ranked minute costs about $0.0008, or 0.08 of a cent. Practice costs $0. I assume a typical student takes one ranked minute per weekday (20 a month) and a heavy user three a day (90 a month).

For a whole school of 1,000 students, everyone a typical user, the model bill is about $16 a month. The binding cost at that scale would be hosting, not tokens. The daily cap, now 300,000 tokens, allows about 47 crewed minutes a day for the whole app. That protects the course key during grading. For a real deployment I would set it from the budget instead: 1,000 typical users need about 4.2 million tokens a day (about $0.54).

What I did to keep cost down, and whether it hurt

  • Practice calls no model. Same road, same clock, $0. It is the default way to just play.
  • Blocked text costs $0. The firewall runs before any model call. The cap checks run before any model call too.
  • Exact work is code. Scoring, the recount, the road, and the caps are deterministic and free. A model would cost tokens and could be argued with.
  • Fewer, smaller round trips. Every model request resends the instructions and the tool list, so the number of requests drives cost. I measured three versions on the same jobs:
VersionSteward + passenger inputClerk inputTotal inputOutputCost / ranked minute
v1 · original release (5 steward tools, rival numbers)5,3203,7539,074437$0.001057
v2 · dropped the duplicate scan tool and unused rival numbers4,3113,9068,217387$0.001015
v3 · steward and clerk batch their independent tool calls3,4802,3795,859419$0.000796

v1 is the original release (one run from the first report plus one re-measured in a fresh-clone dry run). v2 and v3 are four matched runs each on the same four car, seed, and note cases. v1 got about 1,100 cached input tokens per open because its prompts were longer. Automatic prompt caching only starts on prompts of 1,024 tokens or more, and v3's prompts are short enough that caching no longer applies. v3 is still cheaper overall. Repeating an identical clerk request was served from the gateway's cache in under a second with identical counts, so v3's clerk numbers are first-time requests only.

v3 costs about 25% less per ranked minute than v1. Did it hurt? I checked the same four cases on each version:

Quality check (4 cases each)v2 one-by-onev3 batched, first promptv3 final prompt
Coach note names the car4 / 44 / 44 / 4
Coach note names the weather3 / 42 / 44 / 4
Steward used all four tools4 / 44 / 44 / 4
Clerk's points match the server4 / 44 / 44 / 4
Clerk used no invented number4 / 44 / 44 / 4
Tip points at the side with missed coins4 / 44 / 44 / 4

Yes, a little at first. With batching, the steward named the weather in only two of four notes, so the minute felt less specific. I added one line to the steward's prompt (“say the weather from track_card in plain words”), re-ran the same four cases, and got four of four with no change in cost. The other checks held in every version. Four cases per version is a small sample, so I read this as no detectable loss, not as proof of none.

6. Safety

The risks that matter for a shared leaderboard with a text box are: someone talks the agents into something, an agent invents a fact or a number, someone fakes a score, and a bug or a bad actor burns the token budget.

RiskWhat is builtEvidence
Prompt injection in the name or the mind note(1) A server firewall before any model call. (2) The provider's content filter. (3) Prompts that treat every field as data. (4) The passenger never sees the note. (5) Output filtered before display.Figures 8, 10, 11; tests
Agent invents a fact or a numberFacts come only from tools. Every number in the coach note and the clerk's close must appear in a tool result, or that line is replaced with a house line. The clerk's points must equal the server's.Figure 9; tests
Faked scoreThe browser sends a trail, never a score. The server rebuilds the road, replays the trail, and throws out trails that are faster than the car, steer faster than the car, run backwards, skip time, or claim more driving than time has passed. The old /api/score route, which let any request post points, is deleted.Figure 5; tests
Loops and overspendingPer-run request and tool-call caps on each agent. Day caps of 300,000 tokens or 120 agent runs. Ten crewed minutes per driver per day. Past a cap, the minute opens on a house card with no model call.Figure 7; tests

The test suite runs without a model and checks each defense. Output from pytest -v on the submitted code:

What is still possible. A determined person could write a script that produces a fake trail obeying the car's limits and wait out the full minute. That is far harder than editing a number in a request, but it is not impossible. The next step is to send the key presses instead of the trail and re-run the physics on the server. Names are not accounts, so the per-driver cap can be dodged with a new name; the app-wide day cap is the backstop.

7. Impact

Real users. Three classmates in the same recruiting season tried Lane League. What they told me afterwards, paraphrased from our conversations:

  • All three said it works as a mental reset: a short break after which they could go back and keep focusing.
  • One said they liked that the game does not circle back to the boring recruiting and studying themes and is not business-oriented, that they had a lot of fun with it, and that it adds fuel to their life.
  • One suggested inviting car companies to sponsor it with advertising, as a way to keep improving the game.

What changed because of them. The comment about recruiting and studying changed the product. The steward and the clerk are now told not to give advice about work, recruiting, or studying. The steward acknowledges the note in a few words and moves to the car (Figure 4), and the clerk talks only about the drive (Figure 5). The sponsorship idea is in Section 8.

Numbers, with where they come from.

MeasureValueSource
Length of a break60 s of driving, hard-capped, plus a 3 s countdownThe app's clock and the server's 60 s check

Users who tried it3 classmates; 3 of 3 said it helped them reset and refocusConversations after they played

Sponsorship, as a classmate suggested. A typical user costs about $0.016 a month in model calls. A car brand sponsoring its own car in the garage, as a featured car with its photo and numbers, would need to bring in only that much per active user to pay for the crew. The real costs of a public launch are licensing the car photos and brand names, which the prototype uses as reference images, and hosting.

How strong is this evidence? The cost and timing numbers are measured. The research numbers are published. The user evidence is three people's reactions, paraphrased. I did not time their usual phone breaks or score their focus before and after. That is the most important thing to measure next (Section 8).

8. Limits and next steps

  • Measure the effect, not just the reaction. A one-week pilot with about ten students: log each break's length with Lane League against their usual phone break, and ask one 1–5 focus question five minutes after each.
  • Server-side physics. Send key presses instead of the trail and replay them on the server, so even a careful forger cannot fake a run.
  • Accounts. Sign in with the school's single sign-on so the board and the per-driver cap belong to real people.
  • No wait. The roughly ten seconds before the drive is the slowest part. Start the minute at once with the house line and swap in the coach note when it arrives.
  • Sponsorship. Talk to one car brand about a featured car, after licensing the photos and names.
  • Hosting. Today it runs locally. A hosted version needs a real database and the per-user caps above.
